note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — U-SHAPED GLUME BASES
tiles.details: Follow one upright, relatively compact flowering spike (often partly enclosed by its upper leaf sheath) and magnify two attached rachis nodes. The paired multiflowered spikelets and thickened, often outward-bowed glume bases are stronger evidence than head posture. A Texas A&M comparison describes Canada wildrye as more often nodding with narrower V-like glume bases; hybrids and regional variants can blur both clues. Existing regional source photographs do not constitute a measured Hays voucher. Photo route: panel 1 (index 0) shows source-identified curved glume bases, while panels 10–11 (indices 9–10) show actual Texas flowering spikes; the glume macro is not a measured Hays voucher.
tiles.short: On several attached mature spike nodes, look for hard pale glume bases bowing outward like a U.
tiles.status: FIELD CUE — LOCAL MEASURED GLUME-BASE MACRO MISSING

tiles.heading: 02 · TUFT, LIGULE AND AURICLES
tiles.details: Trace an actual rooted shoot: published GrassBase describes a perennial clump, without a creeping rhizome. At the blade/sheath junction inspect the very short membranous ligule and often clasping, curved auricles; these support an Elymus identification, not a definitive separation from E. canadensis. Source photographs show connected roots and flowering culms, but a fresh same-voucher Hays collar with a 1-mm ruler remains unverified. Photo route: panel 8 (index 7) documents connected roots and flowering culms on a Central Texas Bob Harms plate; panel 7 (index 6) shows foliage. Neither image proves a 0–1 mm inner ligule or auricles at a measured collar.
tiles.short: Cool-season tufted perennial, culms about 60–120 cm; membranous ligule 0–1 mm.
tiles.status: PUBLISHED MEASUREMENTS — TRUE COLLAR MACRO NEEDED

tiles.heading: 03 · COUNT SPIKELETS AND FLORETS
tiles.details: Go Botany documents 2–3 spikelets per node and 10–15 mm spikelet bodies. At 10–20× count actual spikelets at ONE node, then open ONE spikelet to find multiple florets; do not count awns as florets. Measure the body without awns and keep the node attached. Hordeum little barley instead has three usually one-flowered spikelets per node, central fertile and lateral often reduced. Photo route: panels 10–11 (indices 9–10) show the spike axis and awned units; panel 1 (index 0) gives an external glume-base close-up. Counting florets and measuring attached node parts still requires a new scaled dissection.
tiles.short: Usually 2–3 sessile spikelets per rachis node, each 10–15 mm with several florets.
tiles.status: SOURCE-BASED ANATOMY — SAME-PLANT NODE SCALE MISSING

tiles.heading: 04 · GLUMES, LEMMA AND AWN ORIGIN
tiles.details: Go Botany reports both glumes 7–15 mm and a lemma awn 3–25 mm; Kew GrassBase describes a 5–25 mm principal lemma awn and a 5–7-veined lemma. Published ranges reflect different treatments and forms. Expose glume body, its awned tip, lemma body and terminal lemma awn separately on one mature dissection. The characteristic hard bowed glume base is not itself a lemma; do not draw anatomy arrows on hidden bracts. Photo route: panel 1 (index 0) illustrates paired curved glumes; panel 11 (index 10) is a flowering close-up, NOT a separated glume/lemma/palea dissection. Do not put microscopic lemma/awn arrows on hidden bracts.
tiles.short: Glumes about 7–15 mm; fertile lemma body about 8–10 mm with one terminal awn often 5–25 mm.
tiles.status: PUBLISHED MORPHOLOGY — DISSECTED MEASURED PHOTO MISSING

tiles.heading: 05 · CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES
tiles.details: Compare mature E. canadensis at the SAME stage: usually longer, spreading awns and straighter V-like glume bases, but E. virginicus × E. canadensis hybrids prevent certainty from one clue. H. pusillum has three one-flowered spikelets per rachis node, versus paired multiflowered Elymus. Nassella leucotricha has a branched panicle of single-flowered, sharply awned units. If attached glumes and head form disagree, retain Elymus sp. and a voucher. Photo route: Virginia panels 1 and 3 (indices 0,2) versus Canada panels 2 and 5 (indices 1,4). The Canada close-up carries a structured depicts/identity discrepancy and must be treated as a provisional comparison, not a voucher-confirmed species diagnostic.
tiles.short: Canada wildrye tends to nod; little barley has one-flowered spikelet triads; Texas wintergrass has a panicle.
tiles.status: COMPARISON KEY — MATCHED VOUCHER PHOTO NEEDED

tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE AND PHOTO HANDOFF
tiles.details: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: same identified Hays-area rooted plant, complete spike and sheath with cm scale; two attached 1-mm-scaled mature nodes with true hard U-bowed glume bases; separately exposed glume, 8–10 mm lemma and its awn; in-focus 0–1 mm true ligule plus auricles; matched E. canadensis V-base specimen. NEEDS_SITE_QA: verify all eight current image records and their original individual CC BY-SA 2.0/Bob Harms credited educational permissions, preserved existing arrows against real pixels, source-label caveats, tile rendering and successful public deployment. Do not change unresolved county-native/hybrid status or claim FINISHED before measured evidence and rights/site QA. Public-readiness route: panels 8, 1, 2 and 10 (indices 7,0,1,9). Verify actual pixels and rights before certifying glume-base annotations; a measured local glume/ligule/lemma series and site QA are still outstanding.
tiles.short: 11 existing teaching panels and 18 markers; measured local glume/ligule/lemma photos and site QA still outstanding.

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: VIRGINIA WILDRYE (Elymus virginicus): first inspect the BASES of the paired GLUMES around one mature spikelet: they are often pale, hard and spread outward like a U. Its seed spike generally stays upright, comparatively compact, with shorter/straighter awns. CANADA typically nods with longer spreading awns and straighter, V-like glume bases. Photograph BOTH the entire head and its glumes—hybrids make single clues unreliable.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: Panel 8 (index 7): begin at Bob Harms's connected fibrous root crown and trace the same original plate to flowering culms; this is real Central Texas root-to-spike evidence, not a Hays voucher.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Follow one upright, relatively compact flowering spike (often partly enclosed by its upper leaf sheath) and magnify two attached rachis nodes. The paired multiflowered spikelets and thickened, often outward-bowed glume bases are stronger evidence than head posture. A Texas A&M comparison describes Canada wildrye as more often nodding with narrower V-like glume bases; hybrids and regional variants can blur both clues. Existing regional source photographs do not constitute a measured Hays voucher. Photo route: panel 1 (index 0) shows source-identified curved glume bases, while panels 10–11 (indices 9–10) show actual Texas flowering spikes; the glume macro is not a measured Hays voucher.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Follow one upright, relatively compact flowering spike (often partly enclosed by its upper leaf sheath) and magnify two attached rachis nodes. The paired multiflowered spikelets and thickened, often outward-bowed glume bases are stronger evidence than head posture. A Texas A&M comparison describes Canada wildrye as more often nodding with narrower V-like glume bases; hybrids and regional variants can blur both clues. Existing regional source photographs do not constitute a measured Hays voucher. Photo route: panel 1 (index 0) shows source-identified curved glume bases, while panels 10–11 (indices 9–10) show actual Texas flowering spikes; the glume macro is not a measured Hays voucher.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Versus E. canadensis: glume bases usually pale, thickened and U-bowed, with a more erect, compact spike and shorter, less divergent awns. E. canadensis tends to nod with longer outward-spreading awns and glume bases that are not distinctly bowed. Intermediate plants and hybrids require additional examination.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: VIRGINIA — actual pale, outward-bowed bony glume bases
panels.caption: At the lowest part of the picture, each group of paired pale glumes bows away from the central point, creating a broad U or cup-shaped basal opening. The slender outer glumes flank hairy inner lemma/floret bodies. Compare Canada wildrye's typically narrower, straighter V-like glume bases, but allow intermediate hybrids.
panels.creator: Matt Lavin
panels.modifications: Original RGB JPEG re-encoded to strip EXIF/GPS
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: CANADA — narrow green glumes beside flowering rachis (CC macro)
panels.caption: Matt Lavin's close source-photographed Elymus specimen highlights long straight-looking narrow glumes, as compared with the outwardly bowed hardened lower glume bases in the adjacent Virginia wildrye photograph. Commons structured 'depicts' metadata is inconsistent with photographer's E. canadensis label (E. wiegandii), so treat comparison as provisionally taxon-labelled and confirm with another source-vouchered specimen. No measurements or exact glume base arrows here.
panels.creator: Matt Lavin
panels.modifications: Original RGB JPEG re-encoded without EXIF/GPS; original pixels not cropped

panels.label: VIRGINIA — upright compact flowering spikes
panels.caption: Three stiffly ascending seed spikes with closely packed awned spikelets. Their posture and compactness support Virginia compared to the looser Canada mature head; photographed spikelets alone are not enough if hybridization is suspected.
panels.creator: Matt Lavin
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: CANADA — two paired spikelets and narrow glumes at a rachis node
panels.caption: Look for the central spike rachis and paired multiflowered spikelets. Long, narrow glumes flank their bases; leaflike bracts enclosing florets are lemmas. This source illustration is about GENUS architecture, not a pixel-proven V-shape glume-base measurement. Wikimedia's taxon depiction metadata is not fully consistent with the original source species label; use as source-labelled teaching reference.
panels.creator: Matt Lavin
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: CANADA — several mature arching/nodding spikes
panels.caption: Mature spikes arc and droop downward; the longer awns spread away from the spike axis. Look for the upper-left and mid-left bent spikes, not the unrelated plants in the background.
panels.creator: Matt Lavin
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.caption: This original archived 'spike' source is actually a broad grass-and-shrub landscape photograph, not a legible mature spike macro. Use as habitat/habit context only. Do NOT attach an erect-spike or glume arrow to it.

Its seed spike generally stays upright, comparatively compact, with shorter/straighter awns. CANADA typically nods with longer spreading awns and straighter, V-like glume bases. Photograph BOTH the entire head and its glumes—hybrids make single clues unreliable.
memory_rule: VIRGINIA = hard pale U-BOWED glume bases + upright tightly packed mature spike. CANADA = straighter narrow V bases + loose drooping long-awned head.
safety_note: Canada comparison macro has an unresolved structured depicts/source-identity discrepancy. The broad Montana Virginia habitat image (panel 6/index 5) is not a diagnostic spike macro. Native target-zone and hybrid holds remain unchanged.
field_rule: Use mature attached glume bases plus spikelet arrangement and overall head habit together; the source-identified Montana glume image and the Texas root-to-spike plate fill different photo roles. Keep ambiguous hybrids as Elymus sp.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.

E. canadensis tends to nod with longer outward-spreading awns and glume bases that are not distinctly bowed. Intermediate plants and hybrids require additional examination.
